title: Yayoi Kusama Dies at 97: Pioneering Avant-Garde Artist Passes Away in Tokyo
text:
Yayoi Kusama, the renowned Japanese avant-garde artist globally celebrated for her signature polka dots, infinite net paintings, and immersive mirror rooms, has died at the age of 97 according to news.yahoo.co.jp. Her studio announced through her official website that Kusama passed away in a Tokyo hospital on August 14. The Guardian reported that the artist reached superstar status after decades living in a psychiatric hospital.
Pioneering Avant-Garde Artist Yayoi Kusama Passes Away at 97
The official studio statement noted that throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant-garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry. The announcement added that she continued working with her paintbrush until shortly before her death, exploring eternal love and the soul across a 97-year life.
Early Life, Childhood Hallucinations, and Move to New York
Born in Matsumoto, Japan, in 1929, Kusama endured a difficult childhood with an abusive mother and a philandering father whose wealthy family managed plant nurseries. As a young child, she began experiencing hallucinations where flowers would swarm around and talk to her, prompting her to draw what she saw as a coping mechanism. At age 13 during the Second World War, she was conscripted to produce fabric for Japanese army parachutes. After studying traditional nihonga painting in Kyoto and rejecting an arranged marriage, she left Japan for New York in 1958.
In New York, she connected with artist and theorist Donald Judd and made a major breakthrough with her “infinity net” paintings—vast fields of impastoed polka dots stretching across canvas. In 1962, she sold her first of these works to artists Frank Stella and Donald Judd for $75. By 2014, her painting White No 28 commanded $7.1 million at auction, setting a record at the time for a living female artist.
Global Artistic Impact and Controversial Happenings
Throughout the 1960s, Kusama pioneered enduring themes centered on infinity and “self-obliteration,” a concept inspired by her engulfing hallucinations. She staged scandalous performance pieces during the hippy era, including “body festivals” with naked performers painted in polka dots, and once wrote to U.S. President Richard Nixon offering to sleep with him in exchange for ending the Vietnam War. At the 1966 Venice Biennale, she presented Narcissus Garden, a display of 1,500 reflective balls sold for $2 each under the banner Your narcissism for sale,
before the biennale shut the operation down.
Kusama returned to Japan in 1973, where she also pursued writing and won the Yasei Jidai New Face Writer Award in 1983 for her novel Christo’s Suicide Cave. She continued producing massive bodies of work, including the My Eternal Soul painting series started in 2009, which yielded approximately 900 pieces over 12 years, followed by the 2021 series I’m Praying for Love Every Day.
Honors, Awards, and Cultural Legacy
Kusama received numerous prestigious honors throughout her career:
- Art Encouragement Prize from the Minister of Education (2000)
- Asahi Prize (2001)
- Officer of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, France (2003)
- Order of the Rising Sun, Gold Rays with Rosette (2006)
- Praemium Imperiale for Painting (2006)
- Person of Cultural Merit (2009)
- Order of Culture (2016)
In 2017, the Yayoi Kusama Museum opened in Shinjuku, Tokyo. Her distinctive pumpkins, polka dots, and large installations have continued to draw immense international attention, including major collaborations with Louis Vuitton and exhibitions at institutions such as the Cincinnati Art Museum, cementing her legacy as a towering figure in modern and contemporary art.

In New York, she connected with artist and theorist Donald Judd and made a major breakthrough with her “infinity net” paintings—vast fields of impastoed polka dots stretching across canvas.
